statement: The system shall generate realistic Gaia data products at different processing stages without requiring the full telemetry and mission-database chain.
The system shall enable users to produce large simulated datasets quickly.
The system shall provide outputs with the appropriate level of realism for the processing stage being studied.
The system shall integrate its outputs into the wider Gaia processing environment without friction.
The system shall handle large data volumes efficiently.
The system shall produce scientifically representative data.
The system shall be compatible with Gaia processing tools.
The system shall remain adaptable as scientific models evolve.
The simulator shall support a defined set of processing stages rather than an open-ended set of stages.
The simulator shall include catalog, auxiliary, intermediate, and a statistically representative final-mission output as candidate processing stages.
The exact list of supported processing stages shall be determined by the project team.
For error models, the user shall be able to choose the model appropriate to the selected processing stage.
For error models, the user shall be able to adjust the main parameters where that makes scientific sense.
The simulator shall provide sensible defaults for error-model configuration.
The simulator shall provide presets for common error-model use cases.
The simulator shall expose advanced error-model controls only to users who need them.
The Gaia Object Generator shall clarify what it needs to do for the science-processing community.
The Gaia Object Generator shall support fast generation of realistic simulated data across the different processing stages.
The system shall support simulated datasets for science testing and pipeline development on the Gaia processing side.
The generator shall be useful to teams that rely on Gaia-like data without requiring them to run the full mission chain every time.
Current generation of realistic Gaia-like data relies on heavyweight simulation or reconstruction chains.
Current generation of realistic Gaia-like data can also use datasets that were produced earlier and then reused.
The current process can be slow and awkward when only a specific processing stage or a different error model is needed.
The current process often requires waiting on other teams or infrastructure.
The system shall be much faster.
The system shall be more flexible.
The system shall allow users to generate the data stage they need directly, without passing through the full telemetry and mission-database workflow.
The system shall let users choose the error models.
The system shall produce data that is statistically representative.
The system shall produce data that is compatible with the broader Gaia environment as the scientific models change.
The system shall remain scientifically useful.
The system shall provide a way to control output size and complexity, enabling generation of anything from small test samples to very large datasets.
The acceptable generation speed shall depend on dataset size.
The selectable error models shall cover the main instrument and processing effects that matter for the data product being simulated.
The current Gaia processing environment shall have existing models and assumptions.
The existing models and assumptions in the current Gaia processing environment are spread across different tools and teams.
There may not be a single source of truth for the existing models and assumptions in the current Gaia processing environment.
The Gaia processing pipeline teams shall be involved as key stakeholders.
Instrument scientists shall be involved as key stakeholders.
Data validation people shall be involved as key stakeholders.
People who run large-scale test production shall be involved as key stakeholders.
The tool shall be stable.
The system shall provide traceability.
Gaia users shall be able to obtain realistic synthetic data for testing, validation, and development without running the full mission pipeline each time.
The system shall generate datasets through a method that is faster and lighter than the normal telemetry and mission-database chain for quick iteration.
The simulator shall support producing catalog-level, auxiliary, intermediate, and final-mission-like data.
The data produced by the simulator shall be statistically representative and compatible with the rest of the Gaia processing environment.
The system shall prioritize speed and flexibility to support model change studies, processing-behavior comparisons, and efficient generation of large datasets as the science evolves.
The system shall handle mission-sized or near-mission-sized synthetic runs.
The system shall be practical for repeated use during development rather than only for one-off studies.
The simulator’s outputs shall be evaluated through manual benchmarking and scientific validation by the users who consume the data.
Teams shall compare runtime, memory use, and output characteristics against previous runs or known reference distributions.
There is no single formal dashboard or acceptance report used consistently by everyone.
The evaluation process depends on the specific working group and the study they are running.
The primary users of the Gaia Object Generator are Gaia science-processing developers and analysts who need synthetic data for testing or model studies.
Configuration of the Gaia Object Generator is usually done by people closest to the simulation or processing framework.
A smaller technical group shall set the processing stage, choose the error models, and tune the run.
Review and approval of the generated data tend to be handled by the relevant science leads or working-group experts.
Review and approval are especially required when the data represent a specific mission phase or when a model change could affect downstream results.
There is no single owner for all of the Gaia Object Generator responsibilities; ownership is distributed across the processing and science teams.
The system shall support advanced developers and simulation specialists who need fine control over inputs, models, and performance.
The system shall provide traceability for specialists.
The system shall support batch automation for specialists.
The system shall enable science users to get the right data products quickly with minimal setup.
The system shall provide a power-user mode.
A simulation run may be initiated on behalf of a science working group that needs a specific scenario checked.
If the output is for a model update, it may go through another review cycle before being accepted as a usable test or science dataset.
The system shall support preparation of the input catalog or source description before simulation execution.
The team shall pass the outputs on to downstream processing or science analysis after review.
If the results do not look right, the team shall adjust the configuration or models and rerun the simulation.
The system shall preserve the full run configuration alongside the output so users can see which stage, model version, and parameter set were used.
Every dataset shall be tied to an immutable record of the exact simulator version used to produce it.
Most metadata and run records are managed through the existing Gaia processing environment.
Metadata consistency over time is a main challenge.
Changes made by different teams to models or configuration conventions can make old runs harder to interpret unless metadata is very disciplined.
Run records must remain accessible for long enough and in a format that still makes sense when the software stack changes.
The Gaia Object Generator should not depend on previous runs in any hidden way.
If caching or intermediate reuse is used for performance, it should be transparent.
The system should handle bad input data as a common problem during simulation runs.
The system should handle missing or inconsistent configuration as a common problem during simulation runs.
The system should handle model/version mismatches as a common problem during simulation runs.
The system should handle failures in downstream components that the generator depends on as a common problem during simulation runs.
The system may provide limited fallback behavior for recoverable issues.
The system may skip a problematic record when handling recoverable issues.
The system may use a default parameter value when handling recoverable issues.
The system's fallback behavior depends on the specific simulation mode.
There is no universal continue-after-error policy across all workflows.
The strictness of each processing stage should be checked to determine error handling behavior.
Each run shall use its own isolated workspace or run directory so that intermediate files, logs, and outputs are not mixed with another execution.
If caching is used, the cache shall be keyed on the exact input and model versions.
For restarts or partial failures, the system shall resume only from well-defined checkpoints and record this in the provenance.
If a run cannot be resumed safely, the system shall discard the partial results and start again rather than risk contaminating the final dataset.
Failures should be isolated to the affected run.
The system should write enough logs and status information to let users see where a run failed.
The system should keep partial output clearly marked so it is not mistaken for a finished product.
For recovery, the system should either restart from a known checkpoint or fail fast and let the user rerun with corrected inputs, depending on the stage.
The system should avoid silently producing incomplete or inconsistent data.
Scientific consistency shall take priority over saving computation.
The system shall follow internal ESA/DPAC data-handling rules rather than external commercial compliance obligations.
The system shall support provenance tracking.
The system shall archive outputs.
The system shall allow the community to trace what was generated.
Each simulation run shall have its own directory tree.
A separate run directory shall make cleanup safer by allowing one run to be inspected or deleted without affecting another run.
Shared resources needed by a run, such as reference models or static lookup tables, shall be read-only and version-pinned.
Generated artifacts shall remain local to the run workspace until the job is complete and validated.
The system shall write checkpoints at well-defined boundaries in the workflow.
Provenance metadata shall record the run ID.
The system shall allow users to determine exactly what was recomputed.
The system shall allow users to determine exactly what was reused.
The system shall allow users to determine whether the final product is scientifically equivalent to a fresh run.
The system shall mark failed or partial runs explicitly in the run status and output metadata.
The system shall ensure that results can be understood unambiguously when reviewed later.
The system shall provide clear run status states for running, completed, failed, and completed with warnings.
The system shall provide an error summary that identifies the stage where the run stopped.
The system shall keep partial outputs in a separate staging area or label them as not for scientific use until the run is formally validated.
The system shall notify the submitting workflow through a job log or message if notification integration is used.
The system shall prevent users from mistaking incomplete data for a finished product.
If any cache-key input changes, the cache entry shall no longer match and the system shall treat the lookup as a cache miss rather than reuse stale data.
Cached products shall carry explicit validity metadata.
If a lookup table or model is superseded, the old cache shall be invalidated in a controlled way.
If there is any uncertainty about compatibility, the system shall recompute instead of trusting the cache.
Checkpoint files shall be treated as serialized run state.
Checkpoint files shall have their own version tag.
Checkpoint files shall include references to the exact software build that created them.
Checkpoint files shall include references to the model set that created them.
Checkpoint files shall include references to the configuration that created them.
On restart, the system shall compare checkpoint identifiers against the current execution context.
The system shall accept a checkpoint only if all identifiers match the defined compatibility rules.
If the code or scientific models have changed in a way that could affect results, the checkpoint shall be rejected automatically or subjected to an explicit, tightly controlled migration step.
If a checkpoint is not accepted, the system shall discard it and restart from the last clean input stage to avoid mixing assumptions across versions.
The Gaia Object Generator shall stream data through the pipeline and write outputs incrementally.
The Gaia Object Generator shall support parallel execution where it is safe to do so.
The Gaia Object Generator shall provide predictable throughput under very large volumes.
The Gaia Object Generator shall keep I/O contention under control.
The Gaia Object Generator shall keep restart overhead under control.
The system shall isolate each run so that a failure in one job does not affect other jobs.
If a worker or stage fails, the scheduler shall retry only the failed unit of work.
The scheduler shall ideally resume a failed unit of work from the last checkpoint.
The system shall not restart everything when a worker or stage fails.
The service layer and execution workers shall be separable for high availability.
If one node goes down, the queue and run metadata shall remain intact.
If one node goes down, another worker shall be able to pick up the job.
Anything that cannot be safely resumed shall be marked failed and left untouched.
The provenance and logs shall show exactly what happened so downstream users do not accidentally consume inconsistent data.
The simulator shall work on copies or mounted snapshots rather than the authoritative source.
A simulation run shall not accidentally change data that other runs depend on.
The system shall enforce access control around run directories and shared repositories.
The system shall perform integrity checks, such as checksums, on inputs and outputs to detect tampering or accidental corruption.
The system should be usable both by core science users who want detailed control and by less technical users who mainly need a sensible default simulation.
The system should provide presets.
The system should provide templates.
The system should provide a straightforward way to choose the processing stage without requiring users to understand every internal model knob.
The system should allow users with limited compute to submit smaller runs.
The system should allow users with limited compute to use a shared execution environment instead of needing local infrastructure.
The system should provide clear defaults.
The system should provide good documentation.
The system should have predictable resource requirements.
The system shall not rely only on a log file to communicate run failure or partial completion status.
The system shall indicate that output files only cover part of the requested interval when a long mission-sized run is interrupted near the end.
The system shall help prevent users from using incomplete or failed outputs in downstream validation or publication work too early.
The system shall provide the run summary in the job control interface to make users aware of run status.
The system should provide automated alerts for failed or partially completed runs.
The system should provide a run dashboard as the main interface for monitoring runs.
The run dashboard should show job state, progress, validation status, and whether outputs are safe to use.
The system should provide email or messaging alerts for failures, exhausted retries, and runs that complete with warnings.
The alerting mechanism should reduce the need for users to continually poll the system.
If the system provides automated interfaces, they should let users drill into the failure reason, identify the failed stage, and quickly find the affected output location.

The notification channel has not been committed to yet and should be verified, with possible options including lightweight web notifications, email, or integration with an existing operations monitor.
The dashboard shall immediately show a simulation run as partial instead of complete when the run succeeds through catalog generation but fails during a later error-propagation stage.
When a run is shown as partial, the system shall let the user stop downstream processing.
When a run is shown as partial, the system shall let the user inspect the failing stage.
When a run is shown as partial, the system shall let the user decide whether to rerun only the failing portion or discard the whole result.
When a resource limit is hit, the system shall send an alert right away.
After a resource-limit alert, the system shall enable users to adjust the requested dataset size or move the job to a larger compute pool before more time is wasted.
The notifications shall steer users to rerun the job, resubmit it with different settings, or hand the issue to operations if the issue appears systemic.
The system shall keep a clear version tag on both the scientific model and the output schema.
The system shall use the version tag to determine what produced a given dataset and what it is compatible with.
When formats or models change, data conversion shall be performed through explicit migration routines rather than ad hoc edits.
The system shall validate converted output against the expected structure and ranges.
The system shall preserve older formats as long as they are still needed.
The system shall provide a documented conversion path so users can regenerate or translate data safely.
For substantial changes, the system shall support rerunning the simulation under the new model instead of patching old outputs.
The system shall preserve scientific meaning when migrating an older output structure to a new one.
The system shall account for changes in parameter names during migration.
The system shall account for changes in units during migration.
The system shall account for changes in error assumptions during migration.
The system shall provide strong validation and clear warnings when a file can be converted but the result is not behaviorally equivalent.
The system shall minimize workflow disruption caused by changes to output conventions.
The system shall maintain compatibility where possible.
Small changes in defaults or rounding rules can shift scientific values enough to break downstream comparisons.
A versioned regression test set should be kept and summary statistics should be compared, not just file validity, before accepting a migration.
Differences in libraries or floating-point handling between platforms can cause the same conversion routine to produce slightly different results.
The processing environment should be pinned as much as possible.
A new release of the Gaia Object Generator shall preserve the ability to read or at least interpret older outputs for a defined support window.
When backward compatibility is not possible, the release shall include a clear deprecation period.
When backward compatibility is not possible, the release shall provide migration guidance.
When backward compatibility is not possible, the release shall ideally provide a conversion tool or a rerun path so users are not forced to rebuild everything blindly.
A release shall include release notes that explain what changed scientifically and operationally.
A release shall provide a way to compare old and new outputs so users can see the impact.
The system shall communicate changes through release notes.
The system shall communicate changes through user documentation.
The system shall communicate changes through direct announcements to the core Gaia processing community.
The system shall provide advance notice before any release that can break workflows.
The system shall provide a summary of what is no longer compatible and what users need to do instead.
The system shall collect post-release feedback through issue reports.
The system shall collect post-release feedback through user support channels.
The system shall collect post-release feedback through direct discussion with the science users who validate the outputs.
The system shall use post-release feedback to inform follow-up patches or the next version.
The system shall prioritize follow-up action when users report repeated conversion problems.
The system shall prioritize follow-up action when users report unclear warnings.
The system shall prioritize follow-up action when users report mismatches between the documented and actual output behavior.
The system shall provide early failure detection with a clear reason for failure.
The system shall identify the stage that failed.
The system shall identify the likely cause of the failure.
The system shall provide an interactive diagnostics view.
The interactive diagnostics view shall show the processing pipeline.
The interactive diagnostics view shall show the error model or input that triggered the issue.
The interactive diagnostics view shall present the relevant logs or validation checks in one place.
The system shall use tiered notifications so routine warnings remain lightweight.
The system shall send detailed alerts only for serious failures or data-integrity problems.
The system shall not send every minor validation note as a separate message.
The system shall avoid notification noise that causes users to ignore the system.
The system shall present a short summary first.
The system shall provide enough detail in the summary to identify the issue.
The system shall provide a link or drill-down to logs, traces, or affected records.
The system shall support user-configurable thresholds or subscription preferences.
The system shall support immediate detailed notifications for some operators and final consolidated reports for others.
The system shall provide visuals that compare expected counts versus actual counts.
The system shall provide visuals that show error distributions.
The system shall provide visuals that show missing-field rates.
The system shall support simulations when users want to test processing ideas.
The system shall support simulations when users want to tune error models.
The system shall support simulations when users need to generate data for scenarios that are too large or too expensive to obtain through the real mission pipeline.
The system shall support simulations when scientists are developing or changing models and need representative datasets before the full chain is available or practical to run.
The system shall address the limitation that the normal telemetry and mission-database workflow is too heavy and too slow for iterative development and large-scale experimentation.
The system shall produce realistic Gaia-like products directly at the relevant processing stage without depending on the full upstream chain every time.
The simulator shall support the main stages of the Gaia processing flow.
The simulator shall support catalog outputs.
The simulator shall support auxiliary outputs.
The simulator shall support intermediate outputs.
The simulator shall support final-mission style outputs.
The simulator shall allow users to choose the processing stage that matches their analysis or testing need.
The simulator shall not force all data through one fixed level of detail.
At the catalog stage, the simulator shall enable evaluation of basic source populations.
At the catalog stage, the simulator shall enable evaluation of whether the synthetic sky content looks plausible for downstream work.
At the auxiliary and intermediate stages, the simulator shall let users test pipeline behavior.
At the auxiliary and intermediate stages, the simulator shall let users test data quality handling.
At the auxiliary and intermediate stages, the simulator shall let users test the impact of different error models or instrument assumptions.
For final-mission style output, the simulator shall produce statistically representative datasets.
For final-mission style output, the simulator shall produce datasets that can be used for validation.
For final-mission style output, the simulator shall produce datasets that can be used for science analysis.
For final-mission style output, the simulator shall produce datasets that can be used for integration testing in the wider Gaia processing environment.
The simulator shall produce outputs that are realistic enough to exercise the science models and processing chain properly.
The main users of the simulation outputs are the Gaia science and processing teams.
Model developers and validation people use realistic data to test changes before those changes are deployed into the wider environment.
Users shall use catalog and intermediate products to check assumptions.
Users shall use catalog and intermediate products to debug algorithms.
Users shall use catalog and intermediate products to compare expected behavior with simulated behavior.
Final-mission style outputs shall support broader validation work.
Final-mission style outputs shall support broader integration work.
Analysts working on instrument performance or error characterization shall use the outputs to explore "what if" cases quickly.
Analysts working on instrument performance or error characterization shall be able to explore "what if" cases without waiting for the full mission database and telemetry chain.
The system shall rely on Gaia-relevant source descriptions as input data.
The system shall rely on instrument and error-model parameters as input data.
The system shall rely on background or population information needed to make the scenario realistic.
The system shall support a fairly simple catalog of sources for a quick test.
The system shall support richer auxiliary information when mimicking a specific processing stage or scientific model.
The system shall vary inputs mainly by level of fidelity and by what the user is trying to validate.
The system shall allow lightweight input for an operational check.
The system shall provide more detailed, scenario-specific source and instrument assumptions when studying a science case or a pipeline sensitivity issue.
Reproducibility is important.
The simulator should keep track of the exact configuration used for a run, including parameter files and the random seed.
If someone reruns the same scenario, they should be able to get the same output or at least trace why it differs if something has changed.
Configuration artefacts should be versioned in a way that makes it clear which scientific model or error model they belong to.
Users should be able to select a saved configuration rather than rebuilding it manually each time.
If the scenario is adjusted, the differences should be explicit so the run is still auditable.
Access to the simulation inputs and outputs should mainly be limited to the Gaia science-processing community and authorized collaborators working on the relevant pipeline or model area.
Users should be able to view outputs only if they are entitled to do so.
Only a smaller set of users should be able to modify shared inputs, configuration, and baseline model definitions.
The system should allow exporting data for use in the wider processing environment.
The simulator's default mode should be fast enough for routine testing and iteration.
The simulator should favor higher scientific fidelity when a run is intended to validate a science model.
In runs that validate a science model, an error model, or a pipeline change that could affect published results, correctness and realism should take priority over turnaround time.
The simulator's speed-versus-fidelity trade-off should vary by stage.
For early catalog or quick operational checks, speed should usually be more important than fidelity.
For intermediate and final-mission style simulations, longer runtimes are acceptable in order to obtain more faithful results, especially when comparing against real mission behavior.
Even when higher fidelity is used, the simulation stage shall remain practical for interactive use and routine validation.
The system shall allow an explicit high-precision validation run in which the user intentionally chooses fidelity over turnaround time.
Outside of explicit high-precision validation runs, the system shall keep a cap on runtime or provide a lighter alternative so teams can iterate.
Earlier-stage simulations, such as catalog or quick intermediate runs, shall stay within minutes to under an hour for normal use.
Heavier final-mission style simulations may take a few hours if they are still intended for routine validation.
If a run is expected to exceed the acceptable runtime threshold, the system shall provide a reduced-fidelity mode as a fallback.

The system shall support a common workflow in which a team selects a Gaia processing stage, chooses the relevant model and error assumptions, generates a representative dataset, and uses the output to test or compare pipeline behavior without running the full mission chain.
The system shall support the end-to-end workflow when users are using a faster fallback mode, provided the output is still good enough for the intended check.
The system shall enable teams to obtain a scientifically credible dataset quickly enough to iterate.
The system shall allow users to reproduce a run later or adapt it cleanly for a new scenario.
The team shall judge credibility by whether the simulated distributions, selected error models, and stage-specific behavior are consistent with the science question or pipeline change being tested.
The simulation results do not need to be a perfect physical replica every time, but they shall be good enough that they are not misleading for the intended use case.
The simulator should keep a run identifier and enough provenance to link the output back to the inputs so that someone else can reproduce or audit the run later.
The system shall provide enough guidance for a scientist to select a stage, choose a sensible preset, and run a simulation without understanding all internal mechanics.
The system shall provide a few guided templates.
The system shall limit self-service setup when a run changes shared baseline models.
The system shall limit self-service setup when a run uses experimental parameters.
The system shall limit self-service setup when a run is intended to support a formal deliverable.
The first rollout shall reliably cover the most common processing stages.
Teams shall use simulation as a normal part of their workflow rather than as a bespoke, engineer-led task.
The workflow shall use more standardized configurations.
The workflow shall require less manual stitching together of inputs to create a test dataset.
Some core Gaia instrument and pipeline stage names shall stay exact.
Label drift shall be avoided because it causes confusion across science and operations teams.
If a stage is renamed over time, the simulator shall preserve the official current label.
The system shall accept older names and aliases as input if they clearly map to one current official label.
If a rename is ambiguous or the mapping has changed across releases, the system shall stop and ask for confirmation rather than guess.
The simulator shall preserve a Gaia label as tentative when the label itself is still provisional in the wider Gaia workflow.
The simulator's saved configuration shall reflect the real state of the science model or pipeline vocabulary at the time of the run.
The simulator shall preserve the published interfaces and file layouts that downstream Gaia tools already depend on.
If an older or provisional structure conflicts with the current structure, the default behavior shall support the official current format.
Validation tolerances shall be tied to the type of output and the intended use of the run rather than using one universal bound.
The simulator shall guide users by asking what they want the data to be used for rather than requiring them to think in internal pipeline terms.
The simulator shall make precedence explicit in the run configuration rather than inferring it from order or names.
If selected models overlap, the simulator shall combine them only when that combination has been defined as valid.
If selected models overlap and no valid combination has been defined, the simulator shall treat the models as mutually exclusive.
A pipeline-stage-specific model shall override a generic default model when both are present.
If there is a risk of double-counting the same effect, the simulator shall suppress one model and log that decision rather than quietly applying both.
If the required inputs are not fully available, the simulator shall stop and mark the run as incomplete rather than producing something that appears finished.
For downstream handoff, the system shall export only outputs that pass the expected format checks.
The system shall tell the user exactly what is missing or mismatched.
Simulation shall be treated as a normal part of the workflow for cases that already rely on it.
Broader or still-evaluated uses of simulation shall remain tentative.
The simulator shall automatically assemble standard, repeatable pieces.
The simulator shall automatically pull the selected stage defaults.
The simulator shall automatically pull the compatible error model set.
The simulator shall automatically pull the usual metadata needed to make the output look like a Gaia product.
The simulator shall infer safe compatibility choices when the user has already provided the key goal of the run.
A person shall provide or verify anything that affects scientific meaning.
A person shall provide or verify special calibration assumptions.
A person shall provide or verify unusual source populations.
A person shall provide or verify a nonstandard downstream target format.
The system shall treat the selected processing stage as a required entity for a run.
The system shall treat the source or population definition as a required entity for a run.
The system shall treat the specific error model or model set as a required entity when the selected stage depends on one.
The system shall treat extra metadata as optional.
The system shall treat convenience defaults that do not change the scientific meaning of the output as optional.
If a needed entity is missing, the simulator shall fail fast and tell the user exactly what is missing.
If a needed entity is ambiguous or incompatible with the chosen stage or error model, the simulator shall not guess silently.
Anything that will be handed off to another tool or used as an official downstream input shall be treated as a firm requirement.
The simulator shall keep a provisional record of outputs for inspection or debugging.
The provisional record shall be very visibly marked as not safe for downstream use.
The system shall accept harmless convenience defaults with a warning.
The system shall block uncertain configuration when it changes the meaning of the data, the stage behavior, or the downstream format until someone explicitly verifies it.
The system shall allow defaults for low-risk, standard items.
The system shall prevent the run from being marked successful when required inputs are missing or incomplete.
The system shall display a clear error message that lists exactly what is missing or incomplete.
The system shall save usable partial results separately as provisional artifacts.
The system shall stop and ask for confirmation if an auto-filled choice would narrow the run to only certain downstream products.
The system shall stop and ask for confirmation if metadata would make the output look valid while actually steering it into a special-case interpretation.
A cosmetic change shall be sent for verification if it could affect how another Gaia tool parses, matches, or validates the output.
A file rename shall be treated as harmless only if the receiving process does not rely on naming conventions.
Reordering fields shall be treated as harmless only if the format is explicitly order-insensitive.

A broad simulation campaign shall generate many statistically useful Gaia-like datasets across different stages and assumptions so scientists can compare models, test processing changes, and prepare downstream workflows without waiting for the full mission chain.
The simulation campaign shall account for the source catalog size as a major scale constraint.
The simulation campaign shall account for the number of error-model combinations as a major scale constraint.
The simulation campaign shall account for repeated generation of intermediate products when exploring parameter space as a major scale constraint.
Storage and export throughput shall be treated as a bottleneck before the actual simulation logic.
The system shall cache a reusable intermediate product and batch the remaining work around it when the intermediate product can be reused without changing the scientific meaning.
The system shall perform full regeneration only when a change invalidates most of the earlier work or when the cached material is more expensive to manage than to recreate.
The gating constraint should be whichever factor is hardest to change without affecting scientific validity.
If the source catalog is fixed by the science case, the source catalog becomes the anchor for the run design.
When the source catalog is fixed by the science case, the system should vary batch size or reuse around the source catalog.
If the source catalog can be reduced without harming the study, the source catalog should be trimmed first.
The gating constraint should be determined by what would force a change in the final interpretation.
The constraint that most changes the meaning of the results should drive the run design.
All other factors should be adapted around the constraint that drives the run design.
Any quota that would risk corrupting or truncating outputs shall be treated as a hard stop.
Compute limits shall be treated as a scheduling constraint rather than a hard stop.
If compute limits cause a run to miss a deadline or starve other priority work, the campaign shall batch more aggressively.
If compute limits cause a run to miss a deadline or starve other priority work, the campaign shall shorten retry loops.
If compute limits cause a run to miss a deadline or starve other priority work, the campaign shall push lower-priority variants to a later window.
An intermediate variant that has been superseded by a confirmed run may be discarded sooner.
Outputs may be archived or compressed earlier when storage pressure starts to interfere with active campaigns.
Outputs may be archived or compressed earlier when they are still useful but not needed for fast access.
Any output needed to reproduce a published result or explain a processing choice shall not be dropped early.
The system shall select the latest approved version that matches the intended processing stage and science use case.
If multiple variants exist, the system shall prefer the version tied to the same validation baseline or campaign context over a newer but unvetted option.
The system shall allow minor operational differences to be overridden if they do not change interpretation.
The anchor should be the factor that defines the science question.
The anchor is usually the source catalog or the processing stage.
After the anchor is fixed, error models, batching, and output handling are adjustable.
A capability should be left out of the current release if it is not needed to produce the core Gaia data products at the chosen processing stage.
A capability should be left out of the current release if it does not block realistic campaign scale or compatibility.
A capability should be deferred if the team can model the science acceptably with a simpler approximation for now.
A capability needs to be included sooner if people cannot validate results without it.
A capability needs to be included sooner if omitting it would make the outputs incompatible with the wider processing environment.
A capability stops being optional if it changes the scientific credibility of the simulator.
A capability stops being optional if it becomes necessary for the main user workflows.
The system may defer a capability only if the approximation remains within the tolerance agreed by the science users for that stage of the pipeline.
If no clear tolerance has been established, the system should not treat the capability as safe to defer.
A capability may remain deferred only if a knowledgeable user would still trust the outputs for validation and comparison without mentally compensating for missing behavior.
If a knowledgeable user would not trust the outputs for validation and comparison without mentally compensating for missing behavior, the capability must be moved up for implementation.
The system shall cap or redesign the element that provides the least scientific value per unit of cost first.
The system shall typically prioritize capping or redesigning repeated intermediate-product generation before extra error-model combinations.
The system shall usually avoid touching the source catalog size before capping or redesigning repeated intermediate-product generation or extra error-model combinations.
The system shall treat output storage or export throughput as the first bottleneck to address when it blocks everything else.
The system shall protect science-defining inputs before constraining operational multipliers.
When tolerance is effectively zero, the system shall check anything that is part of the contract for that release.
When tolerance is effectively zero, the system shall check the schema.
When tolerance is effectively zero, the system shall check the deterministic transform steps.
When tolerance is effectively zero, the system shall check any legacy-reproduction paths that users rely on for comparison.
The schema, deterministic transform steps, and legacy-reproduction paths that users rely on for comparison shall match exactly or match within a very narrowly defined documented exception.
Minor differences are acceptable only if they are purely non-scientific.
Minor differences such as ordering that does not affect interpretation are acceptable.
Minor differences such as metadata timestamps are acceptable.
Minor differences such as formatting that does not change the content are acceptable.
Anything that could alter a downstream result or break reproducibility shall be treated as a failure in that mode.
Anything that changes the scientific interpretation has to be fixed now.
Anything that breaks reproducibility has to be fixed now.
Anything that prevents comparison against reference Gaia processing has to be fixed now.
An issue that is understood and bounded can be recorded as an exception for this release if users can still validate safely with a documented caveat.
An issue that only affects completeness can wait for a later release.
An issue that only affects convenience can wait for a later release.
An issue that only affects a non-critical edge case can wait for a later release.
If the current Gaia assets cannot be consumed or produced without the conversion, the conversion must be done now.
If the data can still move through the workflow with a reliable, documented workaround that users are willing to accept for the first release, the conversion can be deferred.
If the mismatch would only affect a future cleanup or a nicer integration path, the conversion can wait for a later migration step.
The deciding criterion is whether the format issue blocks the core simulator workflow or only makes it less elegant.
When a scientific model is updated, the new behavior shall be introduced in a controlled release.
If a newer scientific model would break compatibility with existing downstream Gaia processing, the system shall preserve the older path or provide a switch until the wider environment has caught up.
The system shall support using a shortcut to test or validate a specific processing stage.
The system shall support using a shortcut to generate large representative datasets quickly without requiring the earlier mission systems to be faithful.
The system shall support using a shortcut when the upstream chain is slow.
The system shall support using a shortcut when the upstream chain is unavailable.
The system shall support using a shortcut when the upstream chain is not relevant to the scientific question being asked.
A shortcut shall be acceptable only if the skipped upstream steps are not expected to change the result in a way that matters for the intended use.
The full upstream chain shall be required if the downstream output depends strongly on upstream details for credibility or comparison.
The simulator shall normalize a label only when there is a clearly defined canonical form required by downstream tools and normalization does not lose information about the original label.
When both the original form and the canonical form are important, the simulator shall keep the original label plus a mapped canonical value rather than overwriting the original label.
Every produced result must be traceable back to the exact input configuration and the simulator version that created it.
If the traceability chain cannot be reconstructed, the output should not be treated as fully auditable for comparison or reproduction.
If both the historical form and the canonical form are useful, the system shall store both and treat the original as the source of truth.
